nameStory: The name 'foxglove' comes from the old belief that foxes wore the tubular flowers on their paws like gloves to muffle their steps while hunting. Some say it's actually from 'folk's glove,' referring to fairy folk who were thought to give these flowers to foxes so they could move silently through the forest. The scientific name Digitalis comes from the Latin word for finger, because the flowers fit perfectly over a human fingertip!
description: Purple foxglove is a stunning tall wildflower that looks like nature's own bell tower, with dozens of drooping, tubular purple flowers arranged up a single towering spike. This European native has made itself at home in New England gardens and wild spaces, growing 3-6 feet tall in its second year. The plant spends its first year as a low rosette of fuzzy leaves, then shoots up dramatically to bloom before dying - but not before dropping thousands of tiny seeds to continue the cycle.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive tubular flowers shaped like gloved fingers, drooping downward along one side of a tall spike. Each purple-pink bloom has darker spots inside and fits perfectly over your fingertip - though don't try this as the plant is highly poisonous!

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, soft, velvety leaves that feel like flannel when you touch them (wash hands afterward). The leaves are arranged in a low rosette the first year, then alternate up the flowering stem, getting smaller toward the top.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Unmistakable tall, single flower spike rising 3-6 feet high, with flowers blooming from bottom to top over several weeks. First-year plants stay low as fuzzy leaf rosettes.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small oval capsules split open to release thousands of dust-like seeds that scatter in the wind. The dried seed capsules make a soft rattling sound when shaken.

habitat: Purple foxglove thrives in partially shaded areas with moist, well-drained soil, often appearing along woodland edges, in forest clearings, and abandoned garden sites. In New England, you'll commonly find it in disturbed areas where forest meets field, along old logging roads, and naturalized around old homesteads. It prefers acidic soil and can tolerate full sun in cooler, moister locations.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants emerge as fuzzy rosettes of leaves close to the ground. Second-year plants send up their impressive flower spikes in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time, with the spectacular purple flower spikes dominating the landscape from June through August. Flowers open from bottom to top over many weeks.
seasonality.fall: Spent flower spikes dry to brown stalks topped with seed capsules that split open to release clouds of tiny seeds. Second-year plants die back completely.
seasonality.winter: Only first-year leaf rosettes remain visible, often staying somewhat green under snow cover. Dried flower stalks may persist as brown spikes.

funFact: Purple foxglove is the original source of the heart medication digitalis, which is still used today to treat heart conditions - the same compound that makes the plant deadly poisonous also makes it life-saving medicine when used properly by doctors!
confusionNotes: The tall flower spike might be confused with lupines, but lupines have completely different palm-shaped leaves and flowers that aren't tubular. Remember: foxglove flowers hang like droopy glove fingers, while lupine flowers stick out from all sides of the spike like a bottle brush.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its beauty, purple foxglove is extremely poisonous - all parts contain cardiac glycosides that can be fatal if ingested. Even handling the plant can cause skin irritation in sensitive people, so always wear gloves and wash hands thoroughly after contact. Never burn foxglove plants, as the smoke can be toxic.
compareHints: Purple foxglove is the most common foxglove species in New England and the most likely to naturalize from gardens. Yellow foxglove has cream-colored flowers and is less common, while other foxglove species are rarely encountered outside of specialized gardens. Purple foxglove's drooping tubular flowers and fuzzy leaves make it easily distinguishable from other members of the plantain family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Yellow foxglove stands out from its more common cousin, purple foxglove, by its soft yellow color and larger individual blooms.

Among foxgloves in New England, straw foxglove is distinguished by its pale, cream-yellow flowers that are much smaller and more numerous than the large, bright yellow blooms of yellow foxglove (Digitalis grandiflora).
Woolly foxglove stands out from other foxgloves by its distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves and small, densely-packed cream flowers.
Among the foxglove family, Rusty Foxglove is unique for its rust-brown flowers - Purple Foxglove has pink-purple blooms, while Yellow Foxglove (rarely seen here) has pale yellow flowers.
